## Summary

Eisman treats tariff policy as disruptive but unlikely by itself to overwhelm US resilience. His main concerns are AI capital returns, software-heavy private credit and insurance links. He distinguishes payment-network moats from exposed software, remains skeptical of solar and Warner Bros valuation, and finds Netflix more interesting. Nvidia and Circle operating growth is supported, while Circle reserve interest is dominant rather than its sole revenue. Private-credit transaction ownership, insurance leverage and loss forecasts require further primary verification.

Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.

## Framework and tools

- Focus on growth, funding and related-party incentives across private credit and life insurance.
- Use network effects to distinguish payments from software-disruption fears.
- Separate reported earnings strength from market narrative and valuation.
- Recognize that institutional information advantages do not guarantee outperformance.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Section 122 versus 301 tariffs
- Private-credit fund discounts and redemption restrictions
- Insurance leverage and CLO structure
- Hyperscaler capex and Nvidia valuation
- Organic versus acquired Salesforce growth
- Mortgage lock-in
- Circle reserves and short rates

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
- Recorded February 26, published February 27.
- Montage repeats the later qualified UBS default scenario; Eisman expressly says he does not know whether 15% is realistic.
- Kuvare Asset Management ownership is not automatically ownership or legal control of Kuvare Insurance.
- Viewer GDP/PCE figures are not silently attributed to Eisman.
